@graph.name: TB PCR and CBNAAT (Xpert MTB/RIF)
@graph.description: TB PCR/CBNAAT refers to molecular nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex in clinically appropriate specimens. Certain platforms also detect rifampicin resistance-associated mutations. Tests differ by platform, cartridge and validated specimen type, so the exact QXL test, rifampicin component and specimen availability must be confirmed before booking.

mainEntity.name: What is TB PCR?

acceptedAnswer.text: A nucleic acid amplification test that detects MTB complex genetic material in a suitable clinical specimen.

mainEntity.name: What is CBNAAT?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification testing, often referring to GeneXpert-style automated MTB assays.

mainEntity.name: Is CBNAAT the same as GeneXpert?

acceptedAnswer.text: CBNAAT describes an approach; GeneXpert is a platform. The ordered cartridge and targets must be specified.

mainEntity.name: What is Xpert MTB/RIF?

acceptedAnswer.text: An automated molecular assay detecting MTB complex and genetic markers associated with rifampicin resistance.

mainEntity.name: What is Xpert Ultra?

acceptedAnswer.text: An updated molecular assay with different analytical characteristics and reporting categories, including trace in some circumstances.

mainEntity.name: Can TB PCR detect drug resistance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some assays detect rifampicin or other resistance markers, but not every PCR test reports resistance.

mainEntity.name: What is rifampicin resistance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Resistance to rifampicin, an essential first-line TB medicine; it requires rapid specialist drug-resistant TB evaluation.

mainEntity.name: What does MTB detected mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: MTB genetic material was detected by the validated assay in that specimen; clinicians correlate with disease and prior treatment.

mainEntity.name: What does MTB not detected mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: The assay did not detect MTB genetic material in the tested specimen; it does not fully exclude TB.

mainEntity.name: Can TB PCR be negative when TB is present?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Low bacillary load, extrapulmonary disease, poor specimen quality and some populations reduce sensitivity.

mainEntity.name: Can TB PCR stay positive after treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. DNA from non-viable organisms may persist and should not be read as treatment failure on its own.

mainEntity.name: Is TB PCR useful to monitor treatment response?

acceptedAnswer.text: Routine molecular NAAT is generally not a substitute for guideline-directed culture/smear and clinical treatment monitoring.

mainEntity.name: What is a trace-positive Xpert Ultra result?

acceptedAnswer.text: A low-level molecular detection category requiring special interpretation considering specimen type and previous TB treatment.

mainEntity.name: What does rifampicin resistance indeterminate mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: The test cannot reliably classify resistance, often requiring additional sampling or specialist DST.

mainEntity.name: Is sputum or blood needed for pulmonary TB PCR?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sputum is the usual specimen for pulmonary TB. A routine blood TB PCR is not the standard first-line pulmonary pathway.

mainEntity.name: Can saliva be submitted instead of sputum?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Saliva is a poor substitute for true respiratory sputum and may yield misleading results.

mainEntity.name: How should I collect sputum?

acceptedAnswer.text: Follow local infection-control and laboratory instructions; a deep-cough specimen into a sterile leakproof container is commonly requested.

mainEntity.name: Can a child have CBNAAT?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, with paediatric sampling pathways such as induced sputum, gastric aspirate or stool depending on the validated method and programme.

mainEntity.name: Can CBNAAT diagnose lymph-node TB?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can support diagnosis from suitable lymph-node specimens when the assay is validated, but a negative result cannot exclude TB.

mainEntity.name: Can CBNAAT be done on pleural fluid?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some assays may be used on selected extrapulmonary specimens, but performance varies and lab validation is essential.

mainEntity.name: Can TB PCR detect TB meningitis?

acceptedAnswer.text: Testing CSF with validated molecular assays can support diagnosis; suspected meningitis requires urgent treatment-oriented specialist assessment.

mainEntity.name: Is chest X-ray enough to diagnose TB?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Imaging supports evaluation but bacteriological testing and clinical assessment are needed.

mainEntity.name: Is AFB smear the same as CBNAAT?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Smear detects acid-fast organisms microscopically and cannot identify MTB or drug resistance with the same specificity.

mainEntity.name: Is TB culture still useful after CBNAAT?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Culture and susceptibility testing may be needed to assess resistance and manage difficult cases.

mainEntity.name: Can GeneXpert diagnose latent TB infection?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Active-disease molecular NAAT is different from infection tests such as IGRA or tuberculin skin tests.

mainEntity.name: Should I isolate while waiting for results?

acceptedAnswer.text: Follow the clinician’s infection-prevention instructions; suspected infectious pulmonary TB may require masking and ventilation precautions.

mainEntity.name: Does a positive CBNAAT mean I can start medicines myself?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Treatment must be prescribed and supervised under appropriate national TB care pathways.

mainEntity.name: Are TB tests available through India’s NTEP?

acceptedAnswer.text: India’s NTEP supports free TB diagnostic and treatment services in public facilities and designated arrangements; ask local programme services.

mainEntity.name: Can the sample be collected at home?

acceptedAnswer.text: Sputum collection and transport may be possible with prior instructions; confirm infection-control suitability and accepted specimens.

mainEntity.name: When is TB evaluation an emergency?

acceptedAnswer.text: Massive coughing of blood, severe breathlessness, confusion or suspected TB meningitis needs emergency care.
